newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy seen in EMU at start of 1999 -- JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: Italy seen in EMU at start of 1999 -- JP Morgan.

text.p: Italy will enter Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) at its start in January 1999 helped by the huge strides the nation has made to improve its finances, an economic research note by brokers JP Morgan said on Monday.
It said the entry of Italy into EMU was also helped by recent budgetary problems in Germany and France, which were blurring the fiscal distinctions among EMU aspirants.

After a very positive first half of 1997, JP Morgan said Italy is closing in on its fiscal goal and may post a deficit of 3.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1997, which is one of the Maastricht criteria for EMU entry.
JP Morgan says that for Italy to stay on course for its three percent 1997 target, the central government deficit needs to be contained at 41 trillion lire in the second half of 1997.
It said that lower debt servicing payments and measures in the Italy's March supplementary budget should yield second-half 1997 savings of around 33 trillion lire.
This should bring the general government deficit down to below 3.5 percent of GDP in 1997, and a 3.0 percent outcome remains possible, the note said.

It said the government could also introduce additional measures by the end of the year, such as bringing forward Value Added Tax (VAT) changes envisaged in the 1998 budget or introducing further cash contraints on monthly Treasury flows.

On the control of pension and other welfare spending, JP Morgan says the government has pledged to keep the ratio of social welfare spending as a share of GDP constant in 1998 at the 1996-97 average. This would mean welfare spending cuts of 10 trillion lire for 1998.
